1.pericope_label: Rejoice not, O Israel, for joy, as other people: for thou hast gone a whoring from thy God, thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor
debates: Whether the reward is given to the idols or received from them
What the rejoicing was actually over
How far the failure of the harvest goes
outliers: Henry says the same sin is not the same offence in a people who were married to God
Calvin makes the taking away of blessings the only method that restores men to a sane mind
Ellicott corrects winepress to wine-vat and fail to deceive, on two old versions
themes: Fires in the streets over a prosperity already ending
Offerings grudged to God and lavished on idols
Starved men standing in the middle of plenty
A harlot who reckons only when the gain stops

3.pericope_label: They shall not dwell in the LORD’S land; but Ephraim shall return to Egypt, and they shall eat unclean things in Assyria
debates: Whether the threat is the cessation of sacrifice in exile or the refusal of sacrifice now
Whether the Lord’s land means Jerusalem, Judea, or the whole land of promise
What makes exile worse than famine
outliers: Calvin makes the unclean food, not the hunger, the dreadful part of the sentence
Ellicott says these verses show Hosea did not treat the northern worship as illegal in itself
Ellicott reaches his rendering only by abandoning the Hebrew accentuation
themes: A land held by the tenure of obedience
A father disinheriting his son
A badge of adoption dropped at the table
Funeral food carried into the house of God

5.pericope_label: What will ye do in the solemn day, and in the day of the feast of the LORD? For, lo, they are gone because of destruction: Egypt shall gather them up, Memphis shall bury them
debates: Whether the flight to Egypt has begun or is still to come
Whether the loss is the sacrifices or the presence they signified
What the silver clause is asking for
outliers: Ellicott turns Memphis into the irony of the passage, the house of the dead they were emancipated from
Clarke reports that those left behind kept the true worship imperfectly and schismatically
Calvin reads the absence of nettles from inhabited ground as a measure of the exile
themes: Trumpets that no longer sound from the whole land
A festival kept in a country of strangers
A refuge that turns out to be a sepulchre
Bought villas standing under nettles

7.pericope_label: The days of visitation are come, the days of recompence are come; Israel shall know it: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad
debates: Whether the fool and the madman are the false prophets or the true one
Whether a verb must be supplied to make sense of the watchman
Why God let the flatterers be believed
outliers: Ellicott ends by saying no rendering yet proposed has any decisive superiority
Calvin rejects an exposition he approves in substance because the words have to be forced
Ellicott would read Ephraim as the people of my God lying in wait
themes: A school where God teaches by the hand, not the mouth
Men rocked asleep in their security
A prophet driven distracted by his own hearers
A watch-tower used to spot prey

9.pericope_label: They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah: therefore he will remember their iniquity, he will visit their sins. I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness
debates: Whether the days of Gibeah mean the outrage or the asking of a king
Whether the finding implies anything found in the people
What the shame in the last clause stands for
outliers: Calvin says the hand is extended in vain to a man already sinking in a shipwreck
Gill holds that what is good in the converted is not found in them but put there
Ellicott reads the word for shame as a substitute for the name of the idol
themes: Roots too deep to be pulled out
A city near the temple site behaving worse than beasts
A grape found by a traveller in a barren place
A young tree bearing its first fruit

11.pericope_label: As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception
debates: Whether the glory is God, or their wealth, or their posterity
Whether the three terms ascend or run backwards
What the departure at the end of the verse adds to the threat
outliers: Calvin says those who confine the sentence to offspring have narrowed a part standing for the whole
Wesley makes losing God the sadder loss of the two
Henry passes on a conjecture linking the place-name to Golgotha
themes: A glory that leaves like a startled bird
Judgment reaching back past birth to conception
Promising children who will not outlive their parents
Prosperity promised to oneself while God withdraws

13.pericope_label: Ephraim, as I saw Tyrus, is planted in a pleasant place: but Ephraim shall bring forth his children to the murderer. Give them, O LORD: what wilt thou give?
debates: What the comparison with Tyre is actually asserting
How the broken prayer of the second verse should be construed
Whether the pleasant place is a meadow or a resting-place
outliers: Calvin makes Ephraim a tree kept indoors through the winter at great expense
Clarke reads the petition as cut short by the prophetic light before it could be finished
Ellicott reports that the old Greek carries a different text altogether
themes: A fortress in the sea that did not save its people
Gardens raised where men struggle with nature
A petition abandoned halfway through
Barrenness asked for as a mercy

15.pericope_label: All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house
debates: Whether the house is the land, the sanctuary, or the household
Why one place can be charged with all the wickedness of a nation
What became of the wanderers
outliers: Calvin holds corrupted worship more offensive than a life with no religion at all
Ellicott supports his reading of house from an Assyrian usage naming a people and its land together
Clarke passes on a claim that the lost tribes survive among the American Indians
themes: A holy place chosen precisely because it was holy
Religion brought forward as compensation for wickedness
A wife turned out of house and home
A tree torn up by the roots, not merely pruned
